claims.text: Balancing rapid nucleation and atomic diffusion during thermal processing governs the formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
A precisely modulated thermal activation window promotes uniform surface-atom reorganization and consistent alloying.
Conventional unmodified thermal treatment leads to phase segregation, elemental clustering, and uncontrolled morphology.
The starting precursor consists of noble-metal salts or organometallic compounds evenly distributed in a matrix.
Changing the thermal profile can provide an activation window that controls surface-atom diffusion and nucleation.
A targeted hold period in the thermal ramp tunes surface-diffusion kinetics.
Surface atoms at nascent nucleation-site interfaces dictate the integration of multiple metals into a uniform alloy.
The modulated thermal profile delays full-scale diffusion sufficiently for surface atoms to rearrange and combine uniformly.
Uniform surface-atom rearrangement produces homogeneous alloying.
An excessively rapid or uncontrolled nucleation-and-diffusion regime causes early elemental clustering and phase separation.
Early elemental clustering and phase separation produce segregated nanoparticle domains.
Modulated thermal treatment will produce a more uniform elemental distribution than the conventional thermal profile.
Modulated thermal treatment will produce more controlled nanoparticle morphology than the conventional thermal profile.
Modulated thermal treatment will increase surface-atom exposure relative to the conventional thermal profile.
The proposed mechanism applies when thermal kinetics dominate phase formation and alloying in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when chemical reactivity, solvent effects, or other nonthermal variables primarily govern phase behavior.
The quantitative relationship between thermal modulation and homogenization is not established.
Failure of the intervention to yield a statistically significant improvement in both homogeneity and surface-atom exposure relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention says overall temperature and all other processing parameters remain unchanged, but the proposed ramp and targeted hold alter the time–temperature history. This is reconcilable if 'overall temperature' means only peak temperature, but that distinction is not stated.
